Overview

Problem statement & grading rules

Task

Given a full-length song, identify which of 20 artists sang it — a single-label, 20-way classification problem. Two independent solutions are required:

  • Task 1 — traditional ML. Hand-crafted audio features (no learned/pretrained feature extractors) into a classical classifier (kNN / SVM / RandomForest).
  • Task 2 — deep learning, from scratch. An encoder + classifier pipeline, with both parts trained from scratch on Artist20's train split — no pretrained weights anywhere in the graded model.

Evaluation

Every model predicts at the song level: a track is split into non-overlapping 5-second chunks, each chunk gets a 20-way softmax, and the chunk probabilities are mean-pooled into one track-level prediction. We report top-1 and top-3 accuracy (correct label within the model's top-k guesses) throughout.

Grading (per the assignment spec)

ComponentWeight
This report50%
Test-set prediction score50%

Prediction score formula: top1_acc + 0.5 × top3_acc, computed by the TA on the held-out test set (233 tracks) from R13921031.json.

Two TA clarifications that shape this whole report

Task 1's accuracy does not count

The TA grades Task 1 only on whether the feature/importance analysis is reasonable and thorough — not the raw classifier accuracy. We therefore give real slide space to the feature-group ablation and permutation-importance results, not just the accuracy table.

Task 2 must be encoder + classifier, both from scratch

A pretrained encoder — frozen or fine-tuned — is explicitly baseline-only, not eligible as the graded submission, even if it scores higher. This is why our highest-scoring model overall (a frozen speaker-verification encoder, 95.2% top-1) is presented as a baseline, and the graded submission is an ensemble of from-scratch architectures instead.

Dataset

Artist20 and the album-level split

Artist20

20 artists, 1413 tracks total (120 albums), 16kHz mono mp3, full-length songs (not pre-chunked). labrosa.ee.columbia.edu/projects/artistid. This assignment provides a fixed split of 949 train / 231 val / 233 test tracks — we use exactly this split throughout (not a self-generated one; see the prior-year-comparison slide for why that distinction matters).

The 20 artists

aerosmith · beatles · creedence_clearwater_revival · cure · dave_matthews_band · depeche_mode · fleetwood_mac · garth_brooks · green_day · led_zeppelin · madonna · metallica · prince · queen · radiohead · roxette · steely_dan · suzanne_vega · tori_amos · u2

Why the split is done per album, not per track [1]

A naive random track-level split lets tracks from the same album land in both train and validation. Because tracks on one album typically share mixing, mastering, and production choices, a model can then reach high accuracy by memorizing album/production fingerprints instead of the singer's actual voice — a shortcut that would not generalize to a genuinely new recording of that singer. Hsieh et al. (ICASSP 2020) [1] introduced the album-level split specifically to close this loophole: each artist's albums are partitioned so that an entire album (all its tracks) goes to only one of train / val / test.

Album-level split, illustrated

Artist X

Every track from a given album stays on one side of the split. The val split has exactly one held-out album per artist (20 albums total) — no album ever appears on both sides, so a model cannot succeed by keying on production style alone.

Term: SpecAugment [9]

A data-augmentation technique that masks random contiguous blocks of the mel-spectrogram along the time and frequency axes during training (like erasing random rows/columns), forcing the model not to rely on any single narrow time/frequency band. Applied to all mel-spectrogram-input models here; the raw-waveform sample_cnn instead gets gain-jitter and additive-noise augmentation on the waveform directly.

This convention has a direct, measured side effect on confidence — see the Calibration slide

Averaging several independent chunk-level softmax outputs (step 7) mechanically flattens the resulting track-level probability vector, even when every chunk's prediction is correct. This is not a training defect; it is a property of mean-pooling peaked distributions, and it explains why every model in this project is systematically underconfident on val (see the Calibration slide).

Pipeline
4
Task 1 — Traditional ML

Hand-crafted features + classical classifiers

Features (librosa / torchaudio, mean+std pooled per track, StandardScaler)

  • Timbre / MFCC (120 dims): MFCC(20) + Δ + ΔΔ — spectral-envelope / vocal-timbre information.
  • Harmonic / tonal (36 dims): chroma + tonnetz — pitch-class / harmonic content.
  • Sub-band energy / spectral contrast (14 dims): spectral contrast across sub-bands.
  • Spectral shape (8 dims): spectral centroid, bandwidth, rolloff, zero-crossing rate (ZCR).

178 dims total, mean+std pooled to one fixed-length vector per track, then StandardScaler-normalized (zero mean, unit variance per feature) before classification — the assignment's own recommendation to keep feature scales consistent and reduce overfitting on a small dataset.

Classical ML feature extraction (single-threaded librosa HPSS + tonnetz on full-length songs, plus SVC(probability=True)'s internal 5-fold CV) took ~4.5 hours on our training server — noted for reproduction: chunking/parallelizing extraction would be considerably faster.

MFCC alone gets 55.0% — almost the whole story by itself — and removing it costs the most of any single group (59.3%→46.8%, −12.5pp). Spectral-shape features (centroid/bandwidth/rolloff/ZCR) are essentially dead weight for the SVM: removing them doesn't hurt at all (59.3%→59.7%, a marginal improvement).

RandomForest permutation importance, by group

Feature groupMean importance
MFCC / timbre0.232
Spectral contrast0.106
Spectral shape0.047

Confirms the ablation independently: timbral/vocal-tract features (MFCC) dominate, harmonic/key information (chroma/tonnetz) contributes least — sensible, since a backing track's harmony varies far more within one artist's catalog than the singer's own timbre does.

Reading this together

Both diagnostics agree on the same mechanism from two different angles (leave-one-group-out accuracy drop, and RandomForest permutation importance) — the SVM's 59.3% is driven almost entirely by timbral information, is barely helped by harmonic content, and is not helped at all by generic spectral-shape descriptors. This is the analysis the TA is grading, not the accuracy number above it.

Task 2 — Deep Learning, from scratch

Nineteen architectures / ablations, one shared pipeline

Every model below shares the pipeline on the previous slide (encoder → chunk-level softmax → mean-pooled song-level prediction) and is trained from scratch on Artist20's train split only — per the TA's rule, no component anywhere in this table is pretrained.

Method 1 — Music tagging CRNN [2,3]

sota_crnn family: mel-spectrogram → 4 conv blocks → unidirectional GRU → linear classifier, based on Choi et al.'s FCN/CRNN [2,3] via minzwon/sota-music-tagging-models. Also from this repo: short_chunk_cnn (7-block residual CNN [19]), sample_cnn (end-to-end raw-waveform CNN [18]), se_resnet (Squeeze-and-Excitation gating [13]). This family produced the winning single from-scratch model (sota_crnn_wide, next slide).

Methods 2-1 / 2-2 / 2-3 — singer-ID-specific nets

crnn_zain ports Nasrullah & Zhao's CRNN2D [4]; confound_crnn ports Hsieh et al.'s CRNN2D_elu2 [1] — the paper that defines this dataset's own album-level split, plus its vocal-separation (confound_crnn_vocals) and cross-song remix (confound_crnn_remix) ablations; fgnl ports the Fully Generalized Non-Local Network [5].

Prior-year architectures, faithfully re-ported

crnn_nasrullah_faithful/_asp (bidirectional GRU + attention pooling [26] / attentive-statistics pooling [14]), singer_senet (channel-ramped 32→512 SE-ResNet [13]), nonlocal_singernet (classic non-local block [15]) — all three faithfully port our own team's prior-year submission for this same assignment, to test its architectural choices directly rather than trust or dismiss them (see the "closing the gap" slide).

Training-recipe ablations (on sota_crnn)

_narrow/_wide (capacity sweep), _norm (per-sample mel normalization), _attn (attention pooling [26]), _dropblock [10], _adamw_ls (AdamW + label smoothing), _supcon [12], _swa [11], _wide_arcface (ArcFace/AAM-Softmax margin head [16]), _ssl_finetune (from-scratch SimCLR/NT-Xent [17] pretraining on our own train split, then fine-tuned — self-supervised but not external data).

Baselines — pretrained encoders (not graded)

ssl_frontend (frozen MERT [8] + trained head) and speaker_frontend (frozen ECAPA-TDNN [6,7] + trained head) — Method 3 / Baseline 1 in the assignment doc. Included for comparison only, per the TA's clarification that any pretrained component is baseline-only.

Graded submission

A weighted ensemble of 7 of the from-scratch models above (weights grid-searched on val) — not any single architecture. Composition and trajectory on the Ensemble slide.

Task 2
9
Task 2 — What the ablations actually show

Ablation takeaways: helped, hurt, mixed

Helped

  • More capacity (wide, +4.3pp over 1.0× baseline)
  • Per-sample mel normalization (+0.4pp)
  • SSL pretraining (from-scratch SimCLR [17] on our own train split, +0.4pp — a "small positive" as one deep-research engine predicted, far below CLMR's 5.6pp literature reference point)

Hurt

  • Attention pooling (−10.8pp vs. last-GRU-state, on sota_crnn's narrow 32-dim unidirectional GRU) — re-tested on a capacity-matched bidirectional GRU-256 backbone (crnn_nasrullah_faithful) and attention pooling still underperforms sota_crnn_wide's plain last-state pooling. Not a capacity artifact — real evidence against full-sequence attention pooling at this task/data scale.
  • Less capacity (narrow, −10.8pp)
  • SupCon auxiliary loss [12] (−2.6pp vs. AdamW/LS-only)
  • DropBlock [10] (−5.6pp vs. AdamW/LS-only)
  • SWA weight-averaging [11] (−3.5pp vs. its own run's best non-averaged checkpoint — averaging made this model worse, not more robust)

Mixed / not clean

  • AdamW + label smoothing alone (75.3%) landed below plain Adam (76.2%) on this exact architecture/width — but every AdamW/LS-based ablation on top of it (norm, dropblock, supcon) used it as a shared base, so it isn't directly isolable; the capacity-sweep (narrow/wide) also used AdamW/LS and still showed channel width as the dominant effect either way.
  • Attentive Statistics Pooling [14] (mean+std) underperformed plain attention pooling on the identical capacity-matched backbone (76.2% vs. 77.9%) — more pooling statistics didn't help here either.

Closing the gap to our own prior-year submission

We re-checked our team's prior-year HW1 submission after it appeared to beat this project's ensemble. Two findings, read together: (1) that submission self-splits train/val by each artist's alphabetically-last album (946/234 tracks) — not this year's official split (949/231) — so the two val accuracies are measured on different tracks and aren't directly comparable; under the assignment's own scoring formula this project's ensemble is not behind (1.305 vs. 1.2995), but that comparison is still cross-split. (2) The prior submission's actual architecture differs from anything in our ablation table at once: bidirectional GRU-256 (vs. unidirectional 32), attention pooling over the full sequence, 4 ConvBlocks up to 256 channels, 10s crops, per-sample mel normalization. We ported it faithfully (crnn_nasrullah_faithful) to isolate architecture from split — result: 77.9%/86.6%, still below sota_crnn_wide's 80.5%/92.2%. Even with the exact capacity and pooling strategy both deep-research engines said was the missing ingredient, it does not beat our winning from-scratch model on this project's official split — the earlier "attention pooling hurt because of backbone capacity" hypothesis does not hold up under this direct test.

14-model-pool ensemble confusion matrix, val set.

An honest limitation of the search itself

A 14-model, 0–2 integer-weight grid search is 314 ≈ 4.78M combinations, evaluated against only 231 val tracks — the largest overfit-to-val risk of any ensemble version tried. The individual models' own numbers remain the more robust per-architecture comparison; read these ensemble weights as "a reasonable combination that measurably helps," not a precisely-tuned optimum. Whether the step-by-step trajectory above is itself statistically meaningful is tested directly on the next slide.

Task 2
11
Task 2 — Statistical rigor

Is any of this actually significant?

The reported ensemble improvements (85.3% → 85.7% → 86.1% top-1 across three versions) are each the size of 1–2 tracks out of 231 val tracks (each track ≈ 0.43pp) — too small to call "confirmed wins" without a test. We ran 5000-resample paired bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar's exact test [20] (both recommended, independently, by four deep-research engines) over five comparisons, re-scoring already-trained models with no retraining.

ComparisonΔ (a − b)Bootstrap 95% CIMcNemar pSignificant?
sota_crnn_wide vs. 14-model ensemble−5.6pp[−9.5, −1.7]pp0.011yes
sota_crnn_wide vs. singer_senet0.0pp[−5.2, +5.6]pp1.0no
9-model ensemble vs. 12-model ensemble−0.4pp[−2.2, +1.3]pp1.0no
12-model ensemble vs. 14-model ensemble−0.4pp[−4.3, +3.9]pp1.0no
9-model ensemble vs. 14-model ensemble−0.9pp[−4.3, +2.6]pp0.81no

What holds up

Ensembling significantly beats the best single from-scratch model (p=0.011) — this is the headline claim this project stands behind. The trajectory of incremental ensemble improvements as each new architecture was added does not individually clear significance at any step — exactly the failure mode the significance testing was designed to catch. The right framing: a structural effect (ensembling beats single models) confirmed via a noisy incremental search path (each step's own gain sits within this val set's noise floor).

A concrete number for the diversity argument

sota_crnn_wide and singer_senet have identical val accuracy (80.5%) but disagree on 40 of 231 tracks (20 each direction) — direct, measured confirmation that two architecturally-unrelated models tied on aggregate accuracy make substantially different individual errors, which is the actual mechanism an ensemble exploits.

Task 2

Error analysis

Calibration: every system is systematically underconfident

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures the average gap between a model's stated confidence and its actual accuracy (15 equal-width confidence bins here). Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted probabilities and the one-hot true label — lower is better-calibrated.

SystemAcc.Mean conf.ECEBrier
sota_crnn76.2%50.7%0.2550.430
sota_crnn_wide80.5%53.3%0.2730.377
14-model ensemble86.1%48.8%0.3730.393
speaker_frontend95.2%46.4%0.4880.373

Counter-intuitive but explained, not a defect

ECE gets worse, not better, as accuracy improves. speaker_frontend is right 95.2% of the time, yet its own predicted probability for its top guess averages only 46.4% — a 49pp gap.

Reliability diagrams, all four systems — every bin sits above the y=x diagonal (observed accuracy > stated confidence) at every confidence level.

Why: a mechanical consequence of song-level mean-pooling, not a training-quality problem

Each track's final probability vector is the mean of many independent 5s-chunk softmax outputs (see the Pipeline slide). Averaging several peaked distributions necessarily produces a flatter one, even when every individual chunk — and the final argmax — is correct. The more chunks a track has, the more this dilutes stated confidence toward uniform, independent of whether the prediction is right. This is a known, explained property of the evaluation convention, worth stating plainly rather than treated as something to fix before submission — and it means the own-voice demo's confidence numbers (later slide) should be read as relative across models on that one clip, not as evidence any model is well-calibrated in an absolute sense.

Error analysis
13
Error analysis

Embedding geometry: cluster quality doesn't track accuracy monotonically

Term: t-SNE [23]

t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding — a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique that projects high-dimensional embeddings (here, each model's per-track representation) into 2D for visualization, trying to keep points that are close in the original space close in the projection. Used for the scatter plots at right; colors mark different artists. A qualitative complement to the quantitative silhouette/distance metrics on this slide.

Silhouette score (Rousseeuw, 1987 [21]) measures, per point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster, averaged over all points; range roughly [−1, 1], higher = cleaner separation. Computed here over cosine distance on track-level embeddings (mean-pooled across a track's chunks, same convention as the t-SNE plots).

ModelVal acc.SilhouetteIntra-distInter-distGap
sota_crnn_wide80.5%0.5100.2300.9710.741
singer_senet80.5%0.3740.2970.7130.416
confound_crnn69.3%0.3440.2600.8920.632
speaker_frontend95.2%0.1800.1660.3240.158

Reported as measured, with no causal explanation invented beyond what the numbers show: speaker_frontend has by far the highest accuracy but the lowest silhouette score and smallest intra/inter gap — its embedding space is more tightly clustered overall (both distances are smallest), yet a downstream head still separates it accurately. Meanwhile sota_crnn_wide and singer_senet are tied on accuracy (80.5%) but have visibly different silhouette scores (0.510 vs. 0.374) — consistent with, though not additional proof beyond, the already-measured fact that these two models disagree on 40/231 val tracks.

Error analysis

Pair-conditional feature importance & vocal-separation attribution

Task 1: what drives the SVM's most-confused artist pairs

For the SVM's top-5 most-confused val artist pairs, a fresh binary SVM was fit per pair and each feature group's permutation importance measured on that pair's own train/val subset (30 repeats/group, Breiman-style group-wise permutation).

PairnBaseline acc.Most important groupΔ
aerosmith vs. green_day2653.8%(none — all negative)—
madonna vs. suzanne_vega2653.8%harmonic/tonal+0.068

Reported honestly, including the noisy/negative results

For aerosmith vs. green_day (and, on timbre/MFCC, madonna vs. suzanne_vega), permuting a feature group raised binary accuracy on that pair's small (22–26-track) val subset. A negative permutation-importance estimate is an expected possibility on subsets this small — it means the estimate is dominated by noise for that pair, not that the feature group is actively harmful. Where a positive signal exists, harmonic/tonal content is the most consistent driver for pairs involving madonna/roxette/aerosmith, and timbre/MFCC separates beatles from cure — reported as the measured pattern, with no further musical interpretation offered beyond what these group names already denote.

Task 2: what a vocal-separation "tie" is actually made of

Demucs [22] vocals-only training (confound_crnn_vocals) tied the raw-mixture confound_crnn exactly on top-1 (67.1% both, pass-1 checkpoints) — but a per-track transition matrix shows this tie hides large, roughly-canceling churn:

Vocals-only correctVocals-only wrong
Raw correct118 (stable)37 (damage)
Raw wrong37 (fix)39 (both wrong)

37 fixed, 37 damaged — an almost exact wash. Per-artist deltas make this vivid: green_day swings +81pp (0%→81%, presumably a dense distorted-guitar mix where separation removes a real confound) while u2 swings −73pp (73%→0%), with prince (−44pp) and fleetwood_mac (−42pp) also damaged. This is consistent with the literature's warning that separation artifacts (musical noise, phase smearing, lost harmonic context) can hurt as much as removing accompaniment helps, per-artist, even when the aggregate looks flat.

The separately-run cross-song remix ablation (confound_crnn_remix, pass-2 pipeline) showed a smaller effect than the literature's ~7–8pp: same top-1 (69.3%), +1.3pp top-3 (84.0% vs. 82.7%) over pass-2 raw-mixture — discussed on the Task-2 results slide.

Inference & visualization — own-voice demo

Mel-spectrogram and inference on an out-of-distribution clip

Input: a Voice Memos recording of "Unstoppable" by Sia (This Is Acting, 2016) — Sia is not one of the 20 trained artists, so this is a genuine out-of-distribution probe, not a memorized track.

Since the graded Task-2 submission is a 7-model ensemble and src/ensemble.py doesn't run this single-clip demo path directly, the demo is run per-model instead:

ModelTop-3 prediction (confidence)
sota_crnn_wide (strongest single from-scratch, current)tori_amos (13.7%), queen (12.9%), fleetwood_mac (12.4%)
sota_crnn (original, superseded)madonna (22.4%), fleetwood_mac (12.4%), roxette (10.8%)
confound_crnn (pass-2)madonna (45.8%), radiohead (17.5%), prince (11.4%)
speaker_frontend (baseline)fleetwood_mac (46.9%), roxette (23.2%), tori_amos (15.9%)

A wider/better model is more uncertain here, not less — the correct qualitative behavior

sota_crnn_wide's top-3 (13.7%/12.9%/12.4%) is a nearly-flat distribution — 20-way chance is 5.0%, so these are barely above it. Across the project's improvement trajectory, confidence in a specific (necessarily wrong, since Sia isn't a label option) answer drops as the from-scratch model gets better: confound_crnn 45.8% → sota_crnn 22.4% → sota_crnn_wide 13.7% on its top pick — small but genuine evidence that later models learn more genuinely discriminative, less-overfit-to-training-idiosyncrasy representations, not just memorize harder.

Across all four runs no two models fully agree, though madonna, fleetwood_mac, roxette, and tori_amos each recur at least twice — with the true singer absent from the 20-class label space, "top-3" reflects each model's own notion of vocal-timbre similarity, not a right/wrong answer.

Own-voice demo
16
Inference & visualization — own-voice demo

Why these artists? A sourced, hedged musicological read

The clip is a Voice Memos recording of someone singing along to Sia's "Unstoppable" (This Is Acting, 2016) — an electropop/anthemic-pop track, not, as our own working notes briefly and incorrectly assumed, part of the Fifty Shades of Grey soundtrack. Sia is broadly documented as having a raspy, dynamically contrasting delivery — restrained, processed verses giving way to forceful, belted choruses. Our models' out-of-distribution top-3 picks are best read as closed-set nearest-class behavior, not identification: with the true artist absent from the 20-class label space, a track's prediction reflects whichever combination of vocal timbre, delivery intensity, and production style the model weighs most heavily, and this varies by model. Across our four runs, one pattern is well-supported: Madonna, the top pick for the two mixture-sensitive models (confound_crnn, sota_crnn), plausibly reflects shared production characteristics (compressed, processed, anthemic pop vocal chain) rather than vocal similarity — the one point every research source consulted agreed on. The other recurring picks are more mixed: Roxette's Marie Fredriksson has an independently-documented vocal profile (wide range, forceful, slightly raspy delivery) that plausibly overlaps Sia's, while the strength of a genuine Sia–Fleetwood Mac vocal parallel is disputed even among sources, and no credible source documents a direct Sia comparison to either Tori Amos or Freddie Mercury specifically. We treat this as a case study in nearest-neighbor behavior under distribution shift, not as evidence any model "recognized" anything about Sia's voice.

Predicted artistAssessmentSource strength
MadonnaProduction/genre artifact, not timbral match — the one point of full cross-source agreementwell-supported (negative)
Fleetwood Mac (Stevie Nicks)Disputed — plausible rasp/delivery overlap per some sources, "production artifact" per othersmixed / contested
Roxette (Marie Fredriksson)Independently-documented vocal traits (range, forceful/raspy delivery) plausibly overlap Sia's, though no source states the comparison directlyplausible, indirect
Queen (Freddie Mercury)Not a register match (baritone-based, documented via peer-reviewed acoustic analysis); more likely a shared-intensity/delivery responsedelivery-level only
Tori AmosNo documented Sia comparison found by most sources; weakest of the fiveweak / unsupported

Explicitly excluded from this report

  • Any precise numeric vocal-range claim (e.g. specific note-to-note ranges) — the sources that gave one were weaker than the sources that explicitly declined to, on both sides of the comparison.
  • The "pop-soul" genre label — traced on inspection to a headphone-review site's user-review page, not a music-genre source; the better-supported label is electropop/anthemic pop.
  • Treating any single predicted artist as a "documented" Sia match.

One AI research assistant (of four consulted for this analysis) asserted several of the excluded claims — including a "direct match" to Fleetwood Mac and to Tori Amos — sourced only to a fan blog; presented here as an unverified claim that did not meet the bar the better-sourced responses set for themselves, not as fact.

Own-voice demo

Baselines — pretrained encoders not the graded submission

How discriminative are off-the-shelf pretrained embeddings?

speaker_frontend (frozen VoxCeleb-pretrained ECAPA-TDNN [6] speaker-verification embedding + trained MLP head, per the speak/sing domain-adaptation premise in [7]) scores 95.2% / 98.7% — dramatically higher than every from-scratch model. Per the TA's rule, this is a baseline only. The interesting claim isn't "speaker embeddings work for singers" (already shown in prior literature); it's that a frozen, off-the-shelf, modern ECAPA checkpoint is already this discriminative with nothing more than a small trained head — no fine-tuning, no separation preprocessing.

Sanity checks (the top follow-up every research source recommended)

EncoderHeadTop-1Top-3
ECAPA-TDNNtrained MLP (original)95.2%98.7%
ECAPA-TDNNlinear probe (no hidden layer)95.2%97.8%
ECAPA-TDNNcosine nearest-centroid (zero trainable params)84.8%92.2%
MERTtrained MLP (original)68.4%—
MERTlinear probe68.8%86.6%
MERTcosine nearest-centroid (zero params)56.7%74.0%

Decisive: a linear probe matches the MLP exactly, and even a parameter-free nearest-centroid classifier gets 84.8% — no trained classifier here is sophisticated enough to be "overfitting" or "memorizing," since one condition has no learnable parameters at all. The ECAPA embedding itself, not the head, carries nearly all the signal. Embedding geometry confirms it: silhouette (cosine) 0.181 for ECAPA vs. 0.001 for MERT; within/between-class cosine-similarity gap 0.158 for ECAPA vs. 0.022 for MERT — MERT's space barely separates artists at all, consistent with its music-domain masked-token training objective encoding general polyphonic structure rather than vocal identity.

speaker_frontend confusion matrix, val — near-perfectly diagonal.

Shuffled-label sanity check (a different failure mode: split/pipeline leakage)

Retrained speaker_frontend with training labels randomly permuted, val labels untouched. Val top-1 collapses to 3.9% (best across 40 epochs: 11.3%), right at the 5.0% chance floor for 20-way classification. The pipeline cannot "cheat" its way to a high score — confirms 95.2% on correctly-labeled data isn't an artifact of a broken split or file-overlap bug.

Caveats not closed out

No access to the true test-set labels (only the TA has them) — val is the best unbiased estimate available, not a locked-test number. No instrumental-only-audio control was run to positively rule out the embedding partly keying on production/instrumentation rather than pure vocal identity.

Bonus — Baseline 2, zero-shot audio-LLM

Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct [25], zero-shot, no gradient steps on this dataset

Prompted with a 15s clip and the closed list of 20 artist names, asked to rank its top-3 guesses — zero training or fine-tuning on Artist20 whatsoever. Evaluated on 40 val tracks (a subsample, not the full 231).

47.5% / 70.0%
top1 / top3, zero-shot

Below the trained models, but surprisingly close to several from-scratch CRNNs (crnn_zain 61.9%, confound_crnn 69.3%), and far above the 5%/15% random-chance floor for 20-way top1/top3 — for a model that saw zero gradient steps on this task.

A parsing-bug lesson worth reporting

The first pass under-scored this baseline at 32.5%/52.5% due to an answer-parsing bug: the prompt asked the model to reply with underscored label names like led_zeppelin, which it naturally spelled as "Led Zeppelin" — the parser didn't normalize spaces vs. underscores before matching. Fixed by presenting space-separated names in the prompt and normalizing both sides before matching. General lesson: always sanity-check an LLM-as-judge or LLM-output parser against a few raw examples before trusting the score — a >15pp swing here came entirely from string normalization, not model capability.

Bonus baseline
19
Honest limitations

What this report does not claim

  • Val, not test. We don't have access to the assignment's held-out test-set labels (only the TA does) — every accuracy number in this report is a validation-set estimate, the best unbiased number available to us, not a locked-test result.
  • Ensemble weight search carries real overfit-to-val risk. The final 14-model, 0–2 integer-weight grid search covers 314 ≈ 4.78M combinations evaluated against only 231 val tracks — the individual models' own numbers are the more robust per-architecture comparison; treat the ensemble weights as a reasonable combination that measurably helps, not a precisely-tuned optimum.
  • Only the aggregate ensembling effect is statistically significant (p=0.011, ensemble vs. best single model). The step-by-step trajectory (9→12→14 models) is not individually significant at any step — reported as a noisy search path, not as three confirmed wins.
  • Vocal-separation/remix effects were smaller than the literature's and not fully disentangled: our remix pairs any two training tracks at random rather than Hsieh et al.'s "different album, same/matched artist" pairing, and the augmentation/LR-schedule fix already captured much of the achievable gain before remix was layered on — both plausible, neither confirmed as the specific cause.
  • Pair-conditional permutation importance is noisy on 22–26-track binary subsets — some negative estimates are reported as-is (see Error Analysis) rather than smoothed into a cleaner-sounding story.
  • No instrumental-only control was run for speaker_frontend, so we cannot positively rule out the embedding partly keying on production/instrumentation rather than pure vocal identity.
  • No separate album-level error clustering is possible from val alone — the val split has exactly one album per artist, so grouping val errors "by album" is mathematically identical to the per-artist breakdown already reported throughout.
  • Two data-integrity incidents were caught and corrected during this project, not swept aside: a queued-tmux-command "ghost retrain" silently overwrote an early confound_crnn checkpoint with a different-seed result, and a frozen-backbone BatchNorm bug let speaker_frontend's "frozen" statistics drift during training (fixed; the properly-frozen version scored higher, 95.2% vs. 89.6%).
  • Not every deep-research claim we consulted was reliable, and we did not treat "two AI sources agree" as validation on its own: one citation backing an ensemble-diversity argument resolved to an unrelated electricity-load-forecasting paper; another (DAMFF, ISMIR 2023) is real but is a music-emotion-regression method, not singer classification, and was flagged rather than built on; several vocal-range and artist-comparison claims traced to a marketing blog and a fan blog and were excluded from the report (see the Sia-demo slide).

pip install -r requirements.txt — torch>=2.6 required throughout (two baseline models' pretrained checkpoints fail to load under HF's safetensors-only torch.load policy on older torch).

Hardware used: 4× H200-NVL-class GPUs / 128 CPU cores, jobs run in parallel via tmux+conda — nothing in the code assumes this; a single modern GPU reproduces every result here serially, and the largest single model comfortably fits on consumer-GPU-class VRAM.

Reproducing the graded submission (exact command)

python -m src.ensemble --data_index_dir data/index \

           crnn_zain:results/crnn_zain/best.pt \

           sota_crnn_norm:results/sota_crnn_norm/best.pt \
           crnn_nasrullah_faithful:results/crnn_nasrullah_faithful/best.pt \

           singer_senet:results/singer_senet/best.pt \
           nonlocal_singernet:results/nonlocal_singernet/best.pt \
  --out_dir results/ensemble4 --max_weight 2 \
  --test_out_path R13921031.json

14 candidate models are passed; the grid search is free to weight any of them to 0 and found the 7-model winning combination (Ensemble slide) on its own. No pretrained weights are downloaded for any component — every parameter in every model was trained on Artist20's train split. For a single-model, no-ensemble reproduction, run sota_crnn_wide alone the same way any other model is run.

Sources deliberately excluded / discounted

Two deep-research citations traced, on inspection, to sources not fit to build on and are named here rather than silently omitted: a citation backing an AI research assistant's ensemble-diversity argument resolved to an unrelated electricity-load-forecasting paper (fabricated/mismatched citation); a second, real citation (DAMFF, ISMIR 2023) is a music-emotion-regression method, not singer/artist classification, and was presented as directly relevant precedent without that mismatch being noted by its source. Neither is cited above or built upon in this report. Several vocal-range and artist-comparison claims about the Sia demo (Own-Voice Demo slides) traced to a marketing blog and a fan blog and are likewise excluded, not presented as sourced fact.
